title: The three colors of fire
hook: look at a flame: the red is heat, the white is water, the black is food, and the 'fire' itself turns out to be a name
carry: name and form, one being beneath
tomorrow: food, water, heat become mind, breath, speech

segments.voice: Yesterday: sat, Being alone, one without a second, becoming heat, water and food. Your line was one Being, without a second, became many.

Light a match and look closely at the flame. It isn't one color. There's a reddish glow, a bright whitish part, and a dark edge where the stick is burning down. Usually it's just fire, blown out before it reaches your fingers. Uddalaka, teaching his son Shvetaketu, looks at the same flame and sees yesterday's creation story, still going on, right there in the colors.
screen: `LIGHT A MATCH.` → `NOT ONE COLOR.` → `THE CREATION STORY, STILL GOING.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Being became heat, water and food. Now Uddalaka says Being entered into them as the living self, the jiva, gave them name and form, nama-rupa, and wove each one together with the other two, so that everything is a braid of three. Then he points to a fire. The red color of fire is the form of heat. The white is the form of water. The black is the form of food, of earth. And then something startling: so the fireness of fire has gone. The change is only a name, a matter of words. The truth is the three colors. That's the clay line from two days ago, word for word, except now the pot is a flame. He does the same with the sun, the moon and lightning: red, white and black in each, and sun-ness, moon-ness, lightning-ness only names. Then he mentions the old teachers. The great householders of old knew this, he says, and so they said: nobody can now tell us anything we haven't heard or thought or known. Whatever they saw that was red, they knew as heat; white, as water; black, as food. Nobody's claiming this is how a modern lab would describe a flame. And it doesn't mean the fire is fake; it still burns. Fire is a name for a form. Hindus still use that pair, nama-rupa, name and form, for the changing surface of things, and under it, the one Being, which entered everything as the living self. Many teachers read that as the root of a central Hindu teaching: the self in you is no stranger to the One.
screen: `EVERYTHING IS A BRAID OF THREE.` · `RED IS HEAT, WHITE WATER, BLACK FOOD.` · `THE FIRENESS OF FIRE HAS GONE.` · `NAMA-RUPA: NAME AND FORM.` · then, large: `NAME AND FORM, ONE BEING BENEATH.`

segments.voice: Look at a candle, a lamp or a sunlit patch of wall, or close your eyes and picture a flame. As you find each color, give it Uddalaka's meaning: red, heat; white, water; dark, food. Then close your eyes and rest in the afterglow, three strands and one flame.
Trivrit, threefold, braided of three. Red for heat, white for water, black for food: Uddalaka's way of seeing every fire, sun and moon this way.
Your line: name and form, one Being beneath. Three strands, and the living self in all of them. Day three hundred forty-two, done.

screen: `DAY 342 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FOOD, WATER, HEAT BECOME MIND.`

howItsDone: The idea that everything is woven of a few basic strands runs through later Hindu thought, including the three gunas of Samkhya and the Gita; some scholars see Uddalaka's three colors as an early forerunner of these ideas, though the link is debated.

fork.setup: you're one of the great householders of old. you've understood the three colors. someone offers to teach you something new about the world. what do you say?

fork.reveal: the text says the old householders said just that: knowing the three, they could see what anything was made of.

original.note: Sanskrit trivṛt: threefold, braided of three. Being made each element trivṛt.

what a scholar hears: Chandogya 6.3–6.4, the trivritkarana or 'making threefold'; it repeats 6.1.4's clay formula with fire, sun, moon and lightning.

chat.says: now Dev says hinduism teaches 'nothing is real, it's all illusion.' Sam looked kinda horrified. is he right??
options: not like that. Uddalaka says 'fire' is a name for a form. it still burns; underneath is one Being, living in everything.
yes: the Upanishads say the world is fake, so nothing you do matters.
no: every fire, sun and moon is its own separate god, real all by itself.
chat.meaning: Uddalaka sees red, white and black in a flame and calls 'fire' a name: underneath are heat, water and food, and the one Being that entered them as the living self.

tie.story: Uddalaka showed his son the red, white and black in a flame and said 'fire' is only a name; the strands are the truth, and Being lives in them.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Sam it isn't 'nothing is real': names and forms change, the one Being beneath them doesn't.

Uddalaka.meaning: Shvetaketu's father, a great teacher of the Upanishads

Shvetaketu.meaning: Uddalaka's son, home after twelve years of study

nama-rupa.meaning: name and form: the changing surface of things

jiva.meaning: the living self in a body

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'most of us just see fire' cut; practice changed so it no longer repeats day 340's name-it-then-let-the-name-go move (now traces each color to heat, water, food).
Hook's description of a match flame (reddish glow, white part, dark edge) is illustrative only; confirm it isn't presented as the text's claim.
'Fire' in 6.4.1 is agni; the three forms rūpa of tejas, ap, anna. Confirm wording.

howItsDone links to the gunas as a later development; confirm this is a fair, non-anachronistic note. Reviewer softened it from 'Vedanta teachers read the three colors as an early form of this' to 'some scholars see ... a forerunner ... debated'; Shankara's own link is to trivrtkarana/pancikarana, not the gunas.

Teach says the fire formula repeats the clay line of 6.1.4 'word for word'; it is the same formula (vacarambhanam vikaro namadheyam ... ity eva satyam) with fire in place of clay. Confirm the claim is fair.
